newsitem.title: SOMALIA: Somalis says aid worker held, charity says all safe.
newsitem.headline: Somalis says aid worker held, charity says all safe.

text.p: Somali businessmen said on Saturday that a British aid worker was being held by gunmen in Somalia but the Save the Children Fund said there was only a "misunderstanding" and that no-one had been kidnapped.
"The report is innacurate. No one has been kidnapped. All our staff are safe and well and we know where they are," Fund spokeswoman Jenny Meadows told Reuters in London.
Meadows said there had been a "minor bureaucratic misunderstanding" on Friday night involving staff in a camp near the border with Ethiopia. "It is inaccurate to call it a kidnap", she said.
Meadows said the Save the Children Fund in London was checking with local field workers to establish what had happened and hoped to get a fuller picture later on Saturday.
Somali businessmen had earlier told Reuters in Mogadishu that an unnamed British woman working with the charity was taken away in the border town of Feerfeer by unidentified gunmen on Friday night.
They said three of her Somali colleagues were also taken.

Aid agency sources in the Kenyan capital Nairobi said talks were being held with a local militia group "to sort out a few misunderstandings," playing down the incident described earlier by local businessmen in Somalia.
"She was taken away by unidentified gunmen yesterday (Friday) afternoon," Abukar Ali, a businessman told Reuters by high frequency radio from Belet-Tuen.
Another one added: "She was taken together with three of her Somali colleagues. We do not know who did it. It could be Somali gunmen or even the Ethiopian army, no-one knows."
Lawless Somalia has been without a central administration since 1991 after rebels ousted late dictator Mohamed Siad Barre.
Kidnappings especially involving foreigners are very common in Somalia, where weapons are readily available.
Aid agency sources in Nairobi said the Fund was holding negotiations with the militia holding the British woman.

"We are not calling it a kidnap. But at the same time they are not free to wander off. They are being held pending negotiations on working and operational procedures in that region," an aid source in Nairobi told Reuters.

Two weeks ago, an Australian pilot held in jail in Somalia for more than four months was freed and flown to Kenya after Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi intervened successfully with south Mogadishu faction leader Hussein Aideed.
